walkthroughs.body_html:
Elements Of Computational Thinking — a core area of A-Level Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Elements Of Computational Thinking brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Elements Of Computational Thinking.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Is cached data always safe to use?
options: No - cached data can become stale when the original source changes, so caching strategies must decide when to refresh or invalidate entries.
Yes - concurrency removes the need for efficient algorithms.
Yes - caches update themselves instantly whenever anything changes.
Yes - once data is cached it is correct forever.

mcqs.q: Does running tasks concurrently always make a program faster?
options: Yes - every program doubles in speed on two cores.
Yes - abstract solutions cannot be implemented as real programs.
No - tasks that depend on each other cannot overlap, and coordination overhead can outweigh gains; only independent work parallelises well.
Yes - concurrency removes the need for efficient algorithms.

mcqs.q: Does abstraction make a solution less correct?
options: Yes - leaving out details always introduces errors.
No - abstraction removes only irrelevant detail; the retained model must stay accurate for the task, like a tube map that is exact about connections.
Yes - abstract solutions cannot be implemented as real programs.
Yes - concurrency removes the need for efficient algorithms.
